scenes.tts: Each outcome so far concerned one protein copy. But a cell controls a whole population. If a kinase writes the mark, why cannot kinase activity alone predict the level? Follow a fixed population while writing and erasing happen together.
scenes.caption: Each outcome so far concerned one protein copy. But a cell controls a whole population. If a kinase writes the mark, why cannot kinase activity alone predict the level? Follow a fixed population while writing and erasing happen together.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's colour map: protein teal, phosphate gold, kinase blue, phosphatase red, ATP violet. Fill the frame with a fixed population of teal protein blocks. A blue kinase adds moving gold badges from the left while a red phosphatase removes them on the right. A blank level gauge waits above.
scenes.narration: Each outcome so far concerned one protein copy. But a cell controls a whole population. If a kinase writes the mark, why cannot kinase activity alone predict the level? Follow a fixed population while writing and erasing happen together.

scenes.visual: Keep gold badges moving between the twelve teal proteins behind the title 'Two Enzymes Set the Level'. The blue and red enzyme arrows remain active.

scenes.tts: Divide the population into an unphosphorylated pool and a phosphorylated pool. The kinase moves available copies toward the phosphorylated side. The phosphatase moves marked copies back. The total number of protein copies stays fixed while membership keeps changing.
scenes.caption: Divide the population into an unphosphorylated pool and a phosphorylated pool. The kinase moves available copies toward the phosphorylated side. The phosphatase moves marked copies back. The total number of protein copies stays fixed while membership keeps changing.
scenes.visual: Transform the carried row into two broad lanes labelled 'unphosphorylated' and 'phosphorylated'. Teal blocks continuously cross under a blue kinase arrow and return under a red phosphatase arrow. Keep a counter on screen labelled 'fixed total'.
scenes.narration: Divide the population into an unphosphorylated pool and a phosphorylated pool. The kinase moves available copies toward the phosphorylated side. The phosphatase moves marked copies back. The total number of protein copies stays fixed while membership keeps changing.

scenes.tts: Use the simplest model: one site, a fixed pool, and effective first-order rates. Kinase flow depends on how many unmarked copies remain. Phosphatase flow depends on how many marked copies exist. A steady level appears when those opposing flows match, although individual copies still cycle.
scenes.caption: Use the simplest model: one site, a fixed pool, and effective first-order rates. Kinase flow depends on how many unmarked copies remain. Phosphatase flow depends on how many marked copies exist. A steady level appears when those opposing flows match, although individual copies still cycle.
scenes.visual: Above the lanes, show the equations 'in = kK(1 − f)' and 'out = kP f' only on screen. Arrow widths update as blocks move. When widths match, the gauge stops rising while individual blocks continue crossing. Label the state 'steady, not static'.
scenes.narration: Use the simplest model: one site, a fixed pool, and effective first-order rates. Kinase flow depends on how many unmarked copies remain. Phosphatase flow depends on how many marked copies exist. A steady level appears when those opposing flows match, although individual copies still cycle.

scenes.tts: Make a prediction. Keep kinase activity fixed but slow the phosphatase. Which way will the phosphorylated fraction move?
scenes.caption: Make a prediction. Keep kinase activity fixed but slow the phosphatase. Which way will the phosphorylated fraction move?
scenes.visual: Freeze neither lane. Keep the blue kinase arrow unchanged and visibly narrow the red phosphatase arrow. Show an empty three-way selector beside the gauge: 'down', 'same', 'up'.
scenes.narration: Make a prediction. Keep kinase activity fixed but slow the phosphatase. Which way will the phosphorylated fraction move?

scenes.visual: Hold the unchanged blue arrow and narrowed red arrow. Teal proteins continue moving slowly. Keep all three selector choices neutral and the gauge blank.

scenes.tts: The fraction rises. Writing now outruns erasing at the old level, so marked copies accumulate. As that pool grows, phosphatase flow also grows. A new steady level appears when the flows match again. Inhibiting an eraser can therefore mimic activating a writer.
scenes.caption: The fraction rises. Writing now outruns erasing at the old level, so marked copies accumulate. As that pool grows, phosphatase flow also grows. A new steady level appears when the flows match again. Inhibiting an eraser can therefore mimic activating a writer.
scenes.visual: Highlight 'up'. Move teal blocks into the phosphorylated lane until the gold gauge reaches a higher plateau. Widen the red flow gradually as its available marked pool grows. Stop when blue and red arrows match again, then show two equal outcome cards: 'kinase up' and 'phosphatase down'.
scenes.narration: The fraction rises. Writing now outruns erasing at the old level, so marked copies accumulate. As that pool grows, phosphatase flow also grows. A new steady level appears when the flows match again. Inhibiting an eraser can therefore mimic activating a writer.

scenes.tts: The balance has a compact rule. At steady state, the kinase rate divided by the sum of both rates gives the phosphorylated fraction. Compute that rule across possible kinase rates. The curve rises smoothly and approaches a ceiling rather than jumping at a fixed threshold.
scenes.caption: The balance has a compact rule. At steady state, the kinase rate divided by the sum of both rates gives the phosphorylated fraction. Compute that rule across possible kinase rates. The curve rises smoothly and approaches a ceiling rather than jumping at a fixed threshold.
scenes.visual: Replace the lanes with a large curve computed from f = kK/(kK + kP), with kP fixed. Label both axes and mark the plot 'computed'. Animate a dot along the curve as kinase rate increases. Keep a small red phosphatase icon fixed beside the plot.
scenes.narration: The balance has a compact rule. At steady state, the kinase rate divided by the sum of both rates gives the phosphorylated fraction. Compute that rule across possible kinase rates. The curve rises smoothly and approaches a ceiling rather than jumping at a fixed threshold.

scenes.tts: The same enzymes also set response speed. Increase both rates by the same factor. The steady fraction stays put because their ratio is unchanged. The population reaches that level faster because the opposing flows are larger. Faster cycling spends A T P faster.
scenes.caption: The same enzymes also set response speed. Increase both rates by the same factor. The steady fraction stays put because their ratio is unchanged. The population reaches that level faster because the opposing flows are larger. Faster cycling spends ATP faster.
scenes.visual: Show two computed time curves from the same starting fraction. They end at the same plateau, but the high-rate curve arrives sooner. Mark both 'computed'. Beside them, speed up equal-width blue and red arrows and make a violet ATP counter fall faster.
scenes.narration: The same enzymes also set response speed. Increase both rates by the same factor. The steady fraction stays put because their ratio is unchanged. The population reaches that level faster because the opposing flows are larger. Faster cycling spends ATP faster.

scenes.tts: A signal can act at either side of the cycle. It may activate the kinase, inhibit the phosphatase, or later activate the phosphatase to end the response. Measuring only the writer misses those possibilities. Measure the substrate's modification and both opposing activities.
scenes.caption: A signal can act at either side of the cycle. It may activate the kinase, inhibit the phosphatase, or later activate the phosphatase to end the response. Measuring only the writer misses those possibilities. Measure the substrate's modification and both opposing activities.
scenes.visual: Return to the two lanes. A signal chip branches to three animations: widening the blue arrow, narrowing the red arrow, then widening the red arrow during shutoff. A measurement bracket expands from the blue kinase alone to include the red phosphatase and the gold-badged substrate pool.
scenes.narration: A signal can act at either side of the cycle. It may activate the kinase, inhibit the phosphatase, or later activate the phosphatase to end the response. Measuring only the writer misses those possibilities. Measure the substrate's modification and both opposing activities.

scenes.tts: Keep the model's boundary visible. It assumes a fixed pool, a single site, and effective first-order rates. Saturated enzymes, several sites, feedback, or protein turnover can change the response. Start with the simple balance, then test whether the system obeys it.
scenes.caption: Keep the model's boundary visible. It assumes a fixed pool, a single site, and effective first-order rates. Saturated enzymes, several sites, feedback, or protein turnover can change the response. Start with the simple balance, then test whether the system obeys it.
scenes.visual: Place the computed curve inside a bright frame labelled 'simple first-order cycle'. Outside the frame, add four muted schematic icons labelled 'saturation', 'multiple sites', 'feedback' and 'turnover'. Do not show outcomes for those extensions. Return focus to the framed balance.
scenes.narration: Keep the model's boundary visible. It assumes a fixed pool, a single site, and effective first-order rates. Saturated enzymes, several sites, feedback, or protein turnover can change the response. Start with the simple balance, then test whether the system obeys it.

scenes.tts: When phosphorylation rises, ask what changed on both sides. More kinase activity is only a possible answer. Less phosphatase activity can produce the same direction of change. The observed level belongs to the cycle, not to either enzyme alone. That is why the substrate measurement matters.
